Your phone gives you four ways to send a message: **typed text**, a **voice note**, a **photo** and a **video**. Most of us use whichever one we are used to. A woman who always types may send three long paragraphs to explain a leaking pipe, when one photo would have done it. A woman who always sends voice notes may send a two-minute recording just to share an account number that the listener must then write down by ear. This course is about choosing well and then doing each format clearly.

Notice that no format is best for everything. Text is precise but cold. A voice note is warm but hard to scan. A photo shows but does not explain. A video shows movement but is heavy on data. Good communicators often **combine** two: a photo of the receipt plus one typed line, or a short voice note plus the account number typed underneath.
Four questions that choose the format for you
**Must the listener copy or keep an exact detail?** (a number, address, date, amount). If yes, that detail goes in text, even if the rest is a voice note.
**Does the message depend on what something looks like?** If yes, add a photo.
**Does it depend on movement, order or sound?** (how to do something, a noise the generator makes, the route from the junction). If yes, a short video.
**Does it depend on feeling or tone?** (thanks, apology, encouragement, a delicate request). If yes, a voice note, or a call.

Still unsure? Call
Ask the questions in order; a single message can pick up more than one format.

There is also a fifth option: **do not record at all**. When a matter is serious, emotional or likely to be misunderstood, such as a disagreement with a family member, a complaint to a landlord about rent, or bad news, a live call or a visit lets the other person respond at once. A recording can be replayed, forwarded and taken out of context. Ask yourself: would I be comfortable if this recording were heard by people I did not send it to?
Worked example: one problem, four possible messages

For example, Halima in Kaduna rents a flat. Water is dripping from the ceiling of her bathroom after rain, and she needs her landlord, an elderly man who prefers calls and voice notes, to send a plumber.
Exact details? Yes: her flat number and the day the leak started. She types: "Flat 3B, leak started Tuesday 14th after the rain."
Looks matter? Yes. She takes two photos: one wide shot showing the whole bathroom ceiling with the stain, and one close-up of the drip with a bucket underneath.
Movement or sound? The drip is visible in the photo, so a video adds little. She skips it to save data.
Feeling matters? He is elderly and likes to be greeted properly, so she records a 25-second voice note: greeting, the problem in one sentence, and a polite request for a plumber this week.
She sends in this order: voice note, two photos, then the typed line, so he hears the greeting first and has the details to show the plumber.
Four short items, chosen on purpose, instead of one long typed paragraph or a rambling three-minute voice note. The landlord can forward the photos and typed line straight to the plumber.
Respect the receiver's situation

Think about where the other person is. Someone in a busy market or an office meeting cannot play a voice note aloud. Someone with weak eyesight may prefer a voice note to small text. Someone on a small data bundle will not thank you for a large video. When you do not know, a short text asking "Can I send you a voice note?" is polite.

Sending a video when a photo would show the same thing.
Sending many separate voice notes of a few seconds each instead of one planned message.
Recording in anger. Wait, calm down, and decide whether a recording is wise at all.

You do not need an expensive phone to communicate well with media. Almost every smartphone sold in Nigeria today, Android or iPhone, has a camera good enough for clear photos in daylight, a microphone good enough for voice notes, and enough storage if you manage it. What matters more is knowing where things are and how much space and data each kind of media takes.
A smartphone
Your phone already holds a recorder, a camera and a gallery; this lesson helps you find and manage them.
Three tools to find today

**Voice recorder.** On many Android phones it is an app called Recorder or Voice Recorder; on iPhone it is called Voice Memos. You can also record voice notes directly inside WhatsApp by holding the microphone button.

**Camera.** Open it and look for the switch between Photo and Video. Find the settings icon (often a gear). Turn on **grid lines**, which divide the screen into nine squares and help you keep pictures straight.
**Gallery or Photos app.** This is where your photos and videos are kept. Open any photo and look for an "i" or "Details" button: it shows the date taken, the file size and sometimes the location.
How heavy is each kind of media?

Roughly, 1,000 KB make 1 MB and 1,000 MB make 1 GB (computers actually use 1,024, but 1,000 is close enough for planning). Your data bundle and your phone storage are both counted in these units. Worked example: will the bundle survive the week?

For example, Ifeoma in Onitsha has 1.5 GB of data left for the week. She wants to send her sister a two-minute video of her new shop, and she also sends about 20 voice notes and 30 photos to customers each week.
She opens the shop video in her Gallery and taps Details: it shows 118 MB.
Voice notes: she checks one of her one-minute notes, it shows about 0.2 MB. 20 notes x 0.2 MB = about 4 MB.
Photos: WhatsApp sends standard-quality photos at a few hundred KB each. She plans for 0.3 MB each: 30 x 0.3 MB = 9 MB.
Total for media: 118 + 4 + 9 = 131 MB. 1.5 GB is about 1,500 MB, so media uses under a tenth of her bundle.
She also notices that if she films the same shop tour three times and sends all three, the video alone becomes over 350 MB. She decides to film once, carefully.
One planned video plus her usual voice notes and photos fits easily. The real danger to her bundle is not voice notes but repeated large videos, auto-downloads and video calls.
Stop WhatsApp from eating your bundle and storage
Open WhatsApp, go to **Settings**, then **Storage and data**.
Under **Media auto-download**, set "When using mobile data" to download nothing, or photos only. Videos and documents will then wait until you tap them.
Under the same menu, look at **Manage storage**. It lists the chats using the most space and lets you review and delete large files, for example old forwarded videos.
In large groups, open the group info and turn off **Media visibility** (on Android) or **Save to Camera Roll** (on iPhone) so group media does not flood your gallery.

On Android, open **Settings** and search for **Storage**. On iPhone, open **Settings, General, iPhone Storage**. You will see how much is used and which apps use the most. Before you clear storage, make sure important photos and voice notes are backed up (Lesson 4.2 shows how). Deleting a chat or clearing WhatsApp media can remove things you cannot get back, such as a receipt photo or the last voice note from a loved one.

If your phone is small, an older model, or shared with your children, a few habits help: close apps you are not using before recording a long video, keep the phone charged above about a third before an event, and carry a clean cloth for the lens. A cheap power bank is often a better investment than a new phone for someone who records a lot.

A photo, video or voice note does not stay where you send it. It can be saved, screenshotted and forwarded to people you will never meet, and it can stay online for years. That is why the habits in this lesson come before any recording skill. They protect you, your children and the people you record.
A person protecting personal information on a screen
Every picture and recording can carry personal information, so you decide what leaves your phone.
Consent: ask, explain, respect the answer

**Consent** means the person agrees, freely and knowing what will happen. Ask before you photograph or record someone, tell them where it will go ("just to my sister", "on our group's Facebook page"), and accept a no without argument. Consent for one use is not consent for every use: a friend who agreed to a photo for your family group did not agree to see it on your business Status. For children, ask the parent or guardian, and think about the child too: a photo that looks sweet today may embarrass a teenager later.

Nigeria has a **Data Protection Act (2023)**, overseen by the Nigeria Data Protection Commission, which protects people's personal information. You do not need to study the law to behave well, but if you collect photos, voice recordings or contact details for a group, business or organisation, treat them carefully and use them only for the purpose you explained.
What your photo can reveal without you noticing

**Location data.** Many phone cameras can save the place a photo was taken inside the file. On Android, open the Camera settings and turn off the option called location tags or save location. On iPhone, go to Settings, Privacy and Security, Location Services, Camera, and choose Never.
**The background.** House numbers, street signs, your children's school badge, a car plate, letters on a table, a calendar on the wall.
**Screens and papers.** A laptop showing emails, an ATM card, a payment alert on another phone.
**Reflections.** Mirrors and windows can show people or rooms you did not mean to include.
Never record or photograph these

Your ATM card number or the three digits on its back, your BVN or NIN, PINs, one-time passwords (OTPs), passwords, and full bank statements. No genuine bank, network or government office will ask you to send these as a photo, voice note or video. If someone asks, treat it as a scam.

Worked example: a birthday photo, checked before posting
For example, Chiamaka in Port Harcourt took a lovely photo of her daughter's seventh birthday party in their sitting room and wants to put it on her WhatsApp Status, which about 300 contacts can see.
Did they agree? Two other children are in the photo. She sends the photo privately to their mothers first; one mother says yes, one prefers not.
She crops the photo so the second child is out of it, using the Crop tool in her Gallery.
Background check: the crop also removes a wall calendar with the school's name printed on it.
Location: she had already turned off location tags in her camera settings.
Audience: in WhatsApp Status privacy she chooses "My contacts except..." and removes business contacts she does not know well.
Final question: would she be fine if a stranger saw it? With the school name and second child removed, yes.
The joy of the day is shared, one parent's wish is respected, and nothing in the picture tells a stranger where her daughter goes to school.
Useful privacy tools in WhatsApp
**View once:** a photo, video or voice note that opens one time and then disappears from the chat. Remember the receiver can still record it with another device, so it is not a guarantee.
**Disappearing messages:** a chat setting that deletes new messages after a chosen time (for example 24 hours, 7 days or 90 days).
**Status privacy:** choose exactly who sees your Status updates.
**Delete for everyone:** works only for a limited time after sending, and the person may already have seen or saved it.

Finally, think about secret recording. Recording a conversation or a person without their knowledge can damage trust and relationships, and in some situations it can bring legal trouble. If you need a record of an agreement, say openly, "Let me record this so we both remember," or follow up with a typed summary the other person can confirm.

When someone sends you a photo, video or voice note of another person, the same respect applies. Do not forward it to a wider group unless the person in it would be comfortable. Many family quarrels start with a voice note forwarded beyond the person it was meant for.

You practise each format with a simple, repeatable method: a voice note that puts the point first, photos that use light, framing, scale and sequence to explain, and a one-minute video that shows directions or steps clearly. Every lesson ends with a real message you send.
The clear voice note: plan, record, listen back, send
Plan a voice note in three parts: point, details, next step
Record without background noise using WhatsApp's lock and preview
Listen back and decide whether to send, re-record or switch format
Keep a voice note to a sensible length for its content

Most unclear voice notes have the same problem: the speaker starts talking before she knows what she wants to say. She greets, explains the background, remembers something else, and only at the end, after a minute and a half, says what she needs. The listener has to replay the whole thing to find the point. The fix is simple: think for ten seconds, then put the point first.
A woman recording a voice note on her phone
A good voice note is planned for ten seconds before the record button is pressed.
The three-part voice note
Three parts of a clear voice note
Greeting and main point
Two or three details
Next step or question
Short close
The listener knows why you are speaking within the first ten seconds.
**Part 1, the point.** After a short greeting, say in one sentence why you are sending this: "Mummy, good morning. I am calling about the date for Ada's naming ceremony."
**Part 2, the details.** Two or three facts only. If there are more, it may need a call or a typed list.
**Part 3, the next step.** What do you want the listener to do, and by when? "Please tell me by Friday if Saturday the 20th works."
**Close.** A short thanks or blessing, then stop. Do not add "OK... so... yes..." at the end.
Recording well in WhatsApp
Move away from the generator, television, traffic and fan. Even a quiet room with soft things (curtains, a bed, clothes) sounds better than a bare room with an echo.
Hold the phone about a hand's length from your mouth, with the bottom of the phone (where the microphone usually is) towards you. Too close makes the sound pop and crackle.
Press and hold the microphone button, then **slide up to the lock** so you can talk without holding your finger down.
Speak a little slower than in normal conversation. Pause between parts. A pause is not wasted time; it helps the listener follow.
Tap **stop** (not send). WhatsApp lets you **play the recording back** before sending. Listen to it, then send, or tap the bin to delete and record again.
Is this voice note too long?

Ask: could the listener act on this without replaying it? A greeting, a date confirmation or a short apology needs well under a minute. An explanation of a decision may need two minutes. If yours is longer than that, split it into a typed list plus a short voice note, or make a call. Listeners can speed up voice notes in WhatsApp, but a well-planned note should not need it.
Worked example: rewriting a rambling voice note

For example, Grace in Ibadan is treasurer of her church women's group. She must tell 40 members that the monthly contribution is now due on the 5th instead of the 10th, starting next month. Her first recording lasts 2 minutes 40 seconds and mentions the new date only at the end.
She listens back and writes down what members actually need: the new date, when it starts, the reason in one line, and where to pay.
Point: "Good evening, my sisters. From next month, contributions are due on the 5th, not the 10th."
Details: "This is because the bank charges us when we pay the hall fee late. The account has not changed."
Next step: "Please reply with a thumbs-up so I know you heard this. If the 5th is difficult for you, call me privately."
She records again: 38 seconds. Underneath, she types: "New due date: 5th of every month, from next month. Same account."
Over the next day, 31 of 40 members reply with a thumbs-up, and only two ask her to repeat the date, compared with many questions after her last long voice note.
A note one quarter of the length, with the key fact typed underneath, gets understood the first time. She keeps the 38-second version as her model for future announcements.
Your voice and your nerves

Many women avoid voice notes because they do not like hearing their own voice. This is very common: your voice sounds different to you in a recording because, when you speak, you also hear it through the bones of your head. Other people hear the recorded version every day and are used to it. Confidence comes from repetition. Record a few practice notes to yourself (WhatsApp lets you message your own number) and listen to them once, looking only for clarity, not beauty.

Speak in the language your listener is most comfortable with: English, Pidgin, Hausa, Yoruba, Igbo or any other. Clarity matters more than grammar. If your group mixes languages, say the key fact in both, or type it.

When you receive a long voice note yourself, you can reply with the same discipline: a short note that confirms the main point ("I have heard you: Saturday the 20th, and I will bring the rice") so the sender knows nothing was missed.

A useful photo answers a question before anyone asks it. When your tailor sees the dress you want copied, can she see the neckline and the length? When the mechanic sees the dashboard light, can he read the symbol? When your mother sees the new baby, is the baby's face bright and sharp? This lesson covers the four things that make photos explain: **light, framing, scale and sequence**.
A woman taking a photo with her phone
Good light and careful framing matter more than the price of the phone.
1. Light
**Use daylight.** Stand near a window or doorway, or go outside in open shade (under a roof or tree, not in direct midday sun).
**Keep the light behind you or to the side**, falling on the subject. If the window or sun is behind the person, their face will be dark.
**Avoid the flash** for most pictures. It makes faces flat and shiny and causes glare on paper and glass.
**Tap the screen on the subject** to focus. On most phones you can then slide your finger up or down to make the picture brighter or darker.
2. Framing
**Wipe the lens** with a soft clean cloth. A fingerprint smear is the most common cause of hazy photos.
**Fill the frame.** Walk closer rather than using zoom; zooming in on most phones loses detail.
**Keep it level.** Use the grid lines you turned on in Lesson 1.2. Line up the edge of a table or doorframe with a grid line.
**Clear the background.** Move bottles, clothes and bags out of the way, or place small items on a plain cloth or sheet of paper.
**Hold still.** Tuck your elbows into your body or rest your hands on a table, and press the button gently.
3. Scale and 4. Sequence

A photo alone cannot show size. A crack in a wall could be the length of a finger or the length of an arm. Put a familiar object beside it: a coin, a biro, a matchbox, your hand, or a tape measure. For things you will sell or report, a tape measure is best because it gives a number.

A single photo often cannot tell the whole story. Professional reporters use a simple **sequence**: a **wide** shot that shows where you are, a **medium** shot that shows the subject, and a **close-up** that shows the important detail. Three planned photos usually explain more than ten random ones.
The three-photo sequence
Wide: where it is
Medium: what it is
Close-up: the key detail
Send the three in this order so the viewer moves from place to detail.
Worked example: asking a tailor to copy a dress
For example, Bisi in Abeokuta wants a tailor 20 kilometres away to sew an ankara dress in the same style as an old favourite. She wants to explain it without travelling.
Light: she hangs the dress on a door near a window at about 10 a.m. and turns off the flash.
Wide: the whole dress, front view, top to hem, with the grid lines keeping it straight.
Medium: the neckline and sleeves together.
Close-up: the back zip and the pleats at the waist, with a tape measure laid across the waist so the tailor can read the width.
Scale: she photographs the tape measure along the full length too; it reads 112 cm from shoulder to hem.
She sends the four photos in order, then types: "Length 112 cm. Same neckline. Pleats at the back only. Fabric: 6 yards, ankara, I will bring it Saturday."
The tailor replies with one question about the sleeve lining instead of asking her to come in. The photos and the typed measurements together do the job of a visit.
When to send in HD or as a document

WhatsApp shrinks photos to save data. For most messages that is fine. When fine detail matters (a document someone must read, a fabric pattern), choose the **HD** option before sending, or send the photo as a **document** to keep the original quality. Both use more data, so use them only when needed.

For documents such as a receipt or a letter, lay the paper flat on a dark, plain surface, hold the phone directly above it so the paper is not slanted, and make sure your own shadow is not on the page. Many phones have a document scanning option in the camera or in apps like Google Drive, which straightens and sharpens the page for you.

Finally, check before you send. Open the photo, spread two fingers to zoom in on the most important detail, and ask: is it sharp, bright enough and easy to read? If not, take it again now, while the subject is still in front of you. A second photo costs a few seconds; going back later can cost a trip.

Video is the right choice when movement, order or sound is the message: how to get to your house from the junction, how to light a new gas cooker safely, how to tie a gele, or what noise the car is making. It is also the heaviest format to send, so the goal is a short, planned video, not a long, wobbly one.

Plan with a shot list

A **shot list** is a short numbered list of what you will film, in order. It stops you from forgetting a step and from filming the same thing twice. For most everyday videos, three to six shots are enough, each lasting 5 to 20 seconds. Write it on paper or in your phone notes before you start.

Filming basics

**Landscape or portrait?** Hold the phone sideways (landscape) for videos people will watch full screen on a TV or laptop. Upright (portrait) suits WhatsApp Status and most phone viewing. Choose one and keep it for the whole video.
**Steady.** Hold the phone with both hands and elbows in, lean against a wall, or rest the phone on a stack of books. Walk slowly, with small steps, when you must move.
**Light.** The same rules as photos: daylight, light falling on the subject, nothing bright behind it.
**Sound.** Switch off the fan and television. Speak towards the phone. Outdoors, wind ruins sound; stand where a wall blocks it.
**Resolution.** In camera settings, 720p or 1080p is plenty for messaging. Higher settings such as 4K make very large files.
Talking while you film

Say what the viewer is about to see, then show it: "Now I turn the knob to the left and hold it down." Name landmarks for directions: "After the mosque, take the second turning on your right, where the blue kiosk is." Keep your fingers away from the microphone. If you make a mistake, pause, say "again", and repeat the sentence; you can cut the mistake out afterwards.

For example, Ngozi in Lugbe, Abuja, is hosting her son's naming ceremony. Guests keep calling her for directions from the main road, which is hard to explain because the last part has no street signs.

She asks her brother to drive while she films from the passenger seat, holding the phone sideways with both hands, filming at 1080p.
She speaks over each shot: "Turn right at this filling station... drive about 300 metres... after the church, the second left... ours is the yellow gate, number 14."
Raw footage is 3 minutes 10 seconds. In the phone's gallery editor she trims the slow parts between landmarks, ending with 1 minute 25 seconds.
Details shows 62 MB on her phone; WhatsApp compresses it when sending.
She posts it in the event group with a typed line and a WhatsApp location pin: "Directions from the main road. Address: No. 14, yellow gate."
Instead of explaining the route on twenty calls, she sends one video with a pin and a typed address. Guests who arrive late can watch it in the car.

Open the video in your Gallery or Photos app and tap **Edit**.

Watch the whole video once with sound before sending. Check: can you hear every instruction, and is anything private in view (a house number you did not mean to show, a person who did not agree)?
Send with a short typed caption saying what the video shows and anything exact, like an address.

Do not film or record voice notes while you are driving or riding. Ask a passenger to film, or stop safely first. Also avoid filming near open flames, hot oil or moving machinery without a second person keeping watch.

If the person you are helping has a small data bundle, offer a choice: "I have made a one-minute video showing the steps; shall I send it now or when you are on Wi-Fi?" For very simple tasks, three photos with numbered captions may do the same job with far less data.

Quality, evidence and honest storytelling

You move from clear messages to media that lasts: photos and recordings kept as a trustworthy record, stories and memories told with care, and media that people with poor sight, poor hearing or limited reading can follow. Sometimes media is not for expression but for **proof**: the condition of a flat when you moved in, goods that arrived damaged, a payment you made, a promise someone made about a date, or a repeated problem such as a broken streetlight reported to the community. A good record is boring on purpose. It is clear, dated, complete and unedited, so that nobody can say you changed it.
A woman organising personal documents

What makes a photo or video trustworthy
**Context.** Start with a wide shot that shows where you are (the building, the room, the shop sign), then the close-up. A close-up alone could have been taken anywhere.

**Date.** Your phone stores the date and time the photo was taken; you can see it in Details. You can also include something that shows the date, such as today's newspaper or a dated receipt, in one photo.
**Completeness.** Photograph all sides of a damaged item, all pages of a document, and the packaging and label of goods that arrived broken.
**No editing.** Do not crop, filter or add stickers to the original. If you need a cropped version to share, make a copy and keep the original untouched.
**A voice description.** A short voice note or video narration on the spot ("It is Monday 3rd, 4 p.m., this is the carton as the rider delivered it") adds clarity.
Build a timeline

For any problem that continues over days or weeks, keep a simple **timeline**: a dated list of what happened, with the photos, receipts and messages that prove each point. Write it in your phone notes or a notebook. Keep entries short and factual, not angry: "12 March: paid N50,000 deposit by transfer, receipt photo saved. 20 March: carpenter promised by voice note to deliver by 30 March."

Worked example: a deposit and a wardrobe that never came

For example, Funmi in Lagos paid a carpenter a deposit for a wardrobe. Weeks later, it has not arrived, and he has stopped replying clearly. She wants an organised record before she involves her estate chairman.
She finds the transfer receipt in her banking app and saves it as a screenshot, then writes the amount and date in her timeline: 12 March, N50,000 deposit of an agreed N120,000.
She scrolls to the carpenter's voice note promising delivery by 30 March and writes down what he said, with the date WhatsApp shows.
She photographs the empty space in her room with the date visible in Details, though this matters less than the payment proof.
She exports the chat: in WhatsApp she opens the chat, taps the menu, More, Export chat, chooses Include media, and saves it to her Google Drive.
She counts the delay: from 30 March to 20 April is 21 days. Her summary line reads: paid N50,000 on 12 March, delivery promised by 30 March, nothing delivered as of 20 April, 21 days late.
She sends the carpenter one calm typed message with the dates and asks for delivery or refund by a named date, then shares the timeline with the estate chairman.
Instead of a long angry voice note, she has a one-page dated timeline backed by a receipt, his own voice note and an exported chat. This is far more persuasive to anyone asked to help.

In Nigeria, the Evidence Act 2011 allows electronic records, such as messages and photos, to be considered by courts under conditions set out in the Act. Whether a particular record is accepted is a legal question. This lesson helps you keep good records; for any court matter, police report or serious dispute, speak to a lawyer, a legal aid service, or a trusted community leader before you act.

Media is not only for instructions and proof. It is also how we keep our grandmothers' voices, celebrate a friend's progress, and share what our women's group achieved this year. A story told well, in a voice note, a set of photos or a short video, can move people in a way a list of facts cannot. This lesson gives you simple tools to tell those stories with care.

The shape of a short story
A three-part story
Before: the situation
Turning point: what changed
After: what is different now
Almost every good short story, from a testimony to a group report, follows this shape.

**Before** sets the scene in a sentence or two: who, where, what was hard. **The turning point** is the moment or decision that changed things. **After** shows the result, ideally with one concrete detail rather than a general claim. "We learned a lot" is weak. "Twelve of us can now open a bank account on our phones" is strong. Keep each part short; for a voice note, the whole story should usually fit in one to two minutes.
Recording an elder's story
**Ask first.** Explain why: "I want the children to hear your stories about growing up in the village." Ask who may listen: only the family, or more widely?
**Choose a quiet place and time** when the elder is rested. Sit close, with the phone on a cloth on the table between you, about an arm's length from the speaker.

**Use open questions** that cannot be answered with yes or no: "Tell me about your wedding day." "What did you do on market days when you were young?" "What do you want your great-grandchildren to know?"
**Listen more than you talk.** Nod instead of saying "yes, yes" over their words. Silence often brings the best memories.
**Record in parts** of 10 to 15 minutes, with a short rest between, using the phone's voice recorder rather than WhatsApp, so a long recording is not cut short or lost in a chat.
**Label each file** straight away with the name, topic and date, for example "Mama Ijeoma, wedding story, 2026-11-02".
Worked example: a five-photo story for a group's year-end
For example, the women's cooperative in Owerri where Uche is secretary wants to show members and supporters what the group did this year, without a long report.
Before (photo 1): the first meeting in January, eight members under a tree. Caption: "January: 8 of us, no savings, meeting under the mango tree."
Turning point (photo 2): the day they opened a group account. Caption: "April: we opened a group account and agreed N2,000 monthly contributions each."
Progress (photo 3): members at a soap-making training. Caption: "July: our first training, paid for from savings."
Progress (photo 4): a table of soap ready for a church sale. Caption: "October: first sale, 60 bars."
After (photo 5): the whole group, now 15 members, in front of a rented stall. Caption: "December: 15 members and our own stall."

Check the numbers: 15 members x N2,000 = N30,000 a month in contributions at full membership. She does not claim a yearly total, because members joined in different months and she has not checked the account statement.
Five photos and five one-line captions tell a clear before, turning point and after story. Every number used is one Uche can show from records, and she leaves out any figure she has not checked.
Testimonies and sensitive stories

Some stories involve illness, loss, family conflict or hardship. Before recording or sharing, agree with the storyteller what will be included, whether their name and face will appear, and who may see it. They can change their mind later, and you should respect that by deleting or not sharing. Never record someone who is distressed and unable to decide calmly.
Small touches that make stories land
Start with a person, not a statistic: one face, one voice.
Use real sounds where they help: the market, a song, children laughing.
Keep captions to one line each, stating a fact the photo cannot show (the date, the name, the number).
End with something the listener can do or feel: a thank-you, an invitation, a lesson.

A family memory project can be as small as one voice note a month from a grandparent, kept in a named folder and shared at family gatherings. Over a year, that becomes a real archive. Over a generation, it may be the only record of how your family spoke, sang and remembered.

Store story recordings as carefully as records. Copy each finished file to a backup folder named for the person or event, and note in a short text file who agreed to what audience. If you ever want to share more widely later, go back and ask again.

Two responsibilities come with sharing media widely. First, make sure the people you want to reach can actually follow it, including those who cannot see well, cannot hear well, or do not read easily. Second, make sure what you pass on is true. A false video forwarded in a family group can cause real panic, and a fake voice note claiming to be from a bank or a government office can cost people money.

Look carefully and say clearly: both make your media easier to follow and harder to fake.

Who
What helps
Someone with poor sight

A voice note, or a caption describing what the photo shows. Phones have screen readers (TalkBack on Android, VoiceOver on iPhone) that read text aloud, but they cannot describe a photo you have not described

Typed summary of any voice note; captions or text on screen in videos; show actions clearly rather than only saying them

**Describing a photo** is a skill. Say what matters, from most to least important, in one or two sentences: "Photo: the new borehole tap at the church gate, painted blue, with a padlock on the handle." Do not start with "Image of"; just describe. This helps blind members of your group and also helps everyone else know what to look for.
Before you forward: stop and check
Five checks before forwarding
Who made it?
When and where?
Does it ask for money or panic?
Do trusted sources confirm it?
Would sharing hurt someone?
If you cannot answer the first four, do not forward it.
**Who made it?** WhatsApp shows a "Forwarded" label, and "Forwarded many times" when a message has passed through many chats. That label means nobody in your chat made it; be extra careful.
**When and where?** Old videos are often reshared as if they were new, or from another country as if they were local. Look for signs, weather, language, vehicles and number plates that do not fit.
**Money or panic?** Messages urging you to act fast, pay a fee, share your BVN, or forward to ten people are classic signs of scams and hoaxes.

**Trusted sources?** Check the official website or verified page of the organisation named. For health claims, check the World Health Organization or the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control. Nigerian and African fact-checkers such as Africa Check and Dubawa publish checks on viral claims.
**Harm?** Even a true video of someone's accident or illness can humiliate them and their family.
Worked example: a scary video in the family group
For example, Rukayat's aunt posts a video in the family WhatsApp group showing a flooded street, with the text "Flood in our area now!! Leave your houses!!" It has the Forwarded many times label.
Who made it? Unknown, and the label shows it has passed through many chats.
When and where? Rukayat pauses the video and notices shop signs in a language and style not used in their town.

Reverse image search: she takes a screenshot of a clear frame, opens Google Lens (in the Google app or Google Photos), and searches it. Results show the same scene in news reports from another country, published years earlier.
Trusted sources: she checks the state emergency management agency's verified social media page and the local radio station's page. Neither reports flooding today.

She replies kindly in the group: "Aunty, thank you for looking out for us. I checked: this video is from another country some years ago. No flood report for our area today. Let us keep watching the state emergency agency's page."
The false alarm stops in her family group without embarrassing her aunt, and the family learns where to check next time.

Today, photos can be edited and voices and faces can be imitated with AI tools. A voice note that sounds like a relative asking urgently for money may not be genuine. Before sending any money, call the person back on the number you already have saved, or ask a question only they would know the answer to.

Hold yourself to the same standard. Never edit a photo or trim a video so that it shows something that did not happen, such as making a product look bigger, hiding a defect from a buyer, or cutting someone's words so they seem to say something else. Honest editing (brightening a dark photo, trimming dead time) is fine. Editing that misleads is not.

You improve fastest when you look at your own work with clear eyes and a few specific questions. Most people send a message and never think about it again, unless something goes wrong. In this lesson you will build three tools: a **quality standard** for each format, a way to **ask for useful feedback**, and a **revision log** that shows your progress over weeks.

Specific feedback and an honest log turn ordinary messages into steady improvement.
A quality standard for each format
Check 1
Check 2
Check 3
Main point in the first ten seconds
No background noise covering words
Next step is clear; key number typed underneath

Score each check 0 (not met), 1 (partly) or 2 (fully met). Each format then has a score out of 6. Do not aim for 6 every time on day one; aim to raise your typical score by one point over a few weeks. The score is for you, not for anyone else.
Asking for useful feedback

"Was it OK?" almost always gets "It was fine." Ask a question the person can actually answer: "Did you understand the new date the first time, or did you have to replay it?" "Could you see the neckline clearly in the second photo?" "Was there any step in the video you could not follow?" Choose someone honest, and thank them even when the answer stings.
Signals you can count
**Follow-up questions.** How many people asked you to repeat or explain? Fewer is better.
**Replays.** Did anyone say they had to listen twice?
**Correct action.** Did people do the right thing: arrive at the right place, pay the right amount, bring the right item?
**Length.** Your voice notes and videos in seconds. Shorter, with the same result, is a sign of clearer planning.
**Time saved.** Calls you did not need to make because the message was clear.

Send again
Change only one thing at a time so you can tell what made the difference.
Worked example: four weeks of a revision log
For example, Aisha in Kano runs a small catering business and sends a weekly voice note menu to 25 regular customers. She wants fewer "What did you say the price is?" messages.
Week 1 (baseline): voice note 2 minutes 10 seconds, prices spoken only. She counts 9 follow-up questions. Self-score 3 out of 6.
Revision 1: she puts "This week's menu and prices" in the first sentence and types the prices underneath. Week 2: 1 minute 30 seconds, 4 follow-up questions.
Revision 2: she records in the store room away from the kitchen generator. Week 3: 1 minute 20 seconds, 3 follow-ups, and one customer says it sounds much clearer.
Revision 3: she adds one photo of the main dish. Week 4: 1 minute 15 seconds, 2 follow-ups, and two new orders mention the photo.
Change in follow-ups: from 9 to 2 is a drop of 7, which is 7 out of 9, about 78 percent fewer questions.
Her log shows clearly which changes helped. She keeps all three revisions as her new routine and records the before and after notes as evidence for her capstone.
Keep the log tiny

A revision log can be one line per message in your notebook: date, format, length, score, follow-up questions, and the one thing you changed. If it takes more than two minutes to fill in, you will stop doing it.

Be fair to yourself. Some follow-up questions come from the listener, not from you: someone was busy, or never reads group messages. Look for patterns over several weeks rather than judging one message. And keep your before versions; listening to your first voice note after a month of practice is one of the best confidence builders there is.
Reviewing photos and videos
**Photos:** look at them on a small screen, the way most people will, and zoom into the key detail. If you have to explain the photo in a long message, it probably needs to be retaken.

**Videos:** watch once without sound. Can you still follow the steps from what you see? Then watch once with sound but without looking. Can you follow from the words alone? A strong how-to video passes both tests.
**Voice notes:** listen at normal speed, once, while doing something else, as your listener will. Note the moment you lost track, if any. That is where to revise.
**Compare old and new:** put version 1 and version 2 side by side and score both with the same checks so the comparison is fair.

Professionals use a rule called **3-2-1**: keep three copies of important files, on two different kinds of storage, with one copy somewhere else. For a phone user this can be as simple as: the original on your phone, a copy in a cloud service such as Google Photos or Google Drive, and, for the most precious files, a copy on a computer or memory card kept at home or with a trusted relative.

Worked example: will 15 GB be enough?
For example, Esther in Jos has a free Google account. Gmail and Drive already use 2 GB. Her phone gallery holds about 3,000 photos and 40 videos she wants backed up.
Space left: 15 GB minus 2 GB = 13 GB, which is about 13,000 MB.

Videos: she checks them and finds they total about 6 GB, or 6,000 MB.

This only works if the backup was switched on before the loss, which is why you set it up today, not after something goes wrong. Typed text carries exact details: numbers, names and times, easy to copy later. A photo shows what something looks like, but does not explain.

Step by step
Four questions choose the format
Exact detail to copy or keep? Type it.
Does it depend on how it looks? Add a photo.
Movement, order or sound? A short video.
Feeling or tone? A voice note, or a call.

First: must the listener copy or keep an exact detail, like a number, an address or an amount? Then that detail goes in text, even if the rest is a voice note.
Second: does the message depend on what something looks like? Then add a photo.
Third: does it depend on movement, order or sound, like the route from the junction? Then a short video.
Fourth: does it depend on feeling or tone, like thanks, an apology or a delicate request? Then a voice note, or a call.
There is a fifth option: do not record at all. A recording can be forwarded and taken out of context. For a quarrel or bad news, call or visit.

When you record an elder, ask first and agree who may listen. Choose a quiet time when she is rested. Ask open questions, like: tell me about your wedding day. Record in parts of 10 to 15 minutes with the voice recorder.
Listen more than you talk, and let silence bring the memories. Never record someone who is distressed. And if a storyteller changes her mind later, respect it.
Before you forward

For example, Rukayat's aunt posts a flood video marked Forwarded many times. Rukayat pauses it and sees shop signs that do not fit their town. Google Lens shows the video is from another country, years earlier.
So run five checks. Who made it? When and where? Does it ask for money or panic? Do trusted sources confirm it? And would sharing hurt someone?
Key points
Remember
Wide shot, close-up, date in the file
Never edit the original; share copies
Describe photos; type a summary of voice notes
Urgent money voice note? Call back first
To remember. Keep records clear, dated and unedited. Tell stories in three parts. Describe photos in words and type a summary under voice notes, for people who cannot see or hear well.
And if a voice note sounds like a relative asking urgently for money, call back on the number you already have saved.

Self-review
Three checks, scored 0 to 2
Voice note: point in the first ten seconds
Photo: sharp, bright, key detail visible
Video: under two minutes, every step audible
Score 0, 1 or 2 per check: out of 6
Ask a question someone can really answer

Each format has three checks. A voice note puts the main point in the first ten seconds, has no noise covering words, and types the key number underneath. A photo is sharp and shows the key detail. A video is under two minutes, steady and audible.
Score each check 0, 1 or 2, for a score out of 6. Do not aim for 6 on day one. Aim to raise your usual score by one point over a few weeks.
When you ask for feedback, do not ask: was it OK? Ask: did you understand the new date the first time, or did you have to replay it?
Worked example
Aisha's four-week revision log
Week 1: 2 minutes 10 seconds, 9 questions
Point first, prices typed: 4 questions
Away from the generator: 3 questions
One photo of the main dish: 2 questions
Change only one thing at a time, and write it down.
For example, Aisha in Kano sends a weekly voice note menu to 25 regular customers. In week 1, her note is 2 minutes 10 seconds, with prices spoken only. She counts 9 follow-up questions.
She puts this week's menu and prices in the first sentence, and types the prices underneath. Week 2 brings 4 follow-up questions.
Next she records in the store room, away from the kitchen generator. Week 3: 3 follow-ups.
Then she adds one photo of the main dish. Week 4: just 2 follow-ups, and two new orders mention the photo.
From 9 questions to 2 is about 78 percent fewer. Because she changed one thing at a time, her log shows exactly what helped. Keep your log tiny: one line per message.
Backups
The copy you carry every day. It can be lost, stolen or dropped in water.
Google Photos or Google Drive. Turn backup on, on Wi-Fi only if data is costly.
For the most precious files: a computer or memory card at home or with a trusted relative.
Professionals use a rule called 3-2-1: three copies, on two kinds of storage, with one copy somewhere else. The first copy is the original on your phone.
The second is in the cloud. In Google Photos, tap your profile picture, open Photos settings, find Backup and turn it on. A free Google account includes 15 GB, shared with Gmail and Drive.
The third, for the most precious files, is a computer or memory card kept at home or with a trusted relative.
Esther checks before she backs up
Space left: 15 GB minus 2 GB = 13 GB
Photos: 3,000 x 3 MB = 9,000 MB
Videos: about 6,000 MB. Total 15,000 MB
Too much: delete duplicates, then back up
For example, Esther in Jos has a free Google account, and Gmail and Drive already use 2 GB. That leaves 13 GB, about 13,000 MB.
Her 3,000 photos average about 3 MB each, which is 9,000 MB. Her videos come to about 6,000 MB. Together that is 15,000 MB, more than she has.
So she deletes about 500 duplicate and blurry photos and 15 forwarded videos, then backs up the rest on Wi-Fi. Simple subtraction first saves a backup that stops halfway.
Protect your backups
WhatsApp and account safety
WhatsApp: Settings, Chats, Chat backup
Strong password on your Google account
Two-step verification turned on
Never share the codes it sends you
Lost phone? Report the line to your network

Your WhatsApp chats need their own backup: Settings, Chats, Chat backup. Anyone who gets into your account can see your photos, so use a strong password, turn on two-step verification, and never share its codes.
If your phone is lost, report the line so your SIM can be blocked.
